title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
tagline: Interphase, the mitotic phases, meiosis as reduction division, and why controlled division matters.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Every new cell arises from an existing cell, and the sequence of events that takes one cell to two is the cell cycle. This chapter separates the long interphase — during which the cell grows and duplicates its DNA — from the short but dramatic phase of cell division itself, then compares the two kinds of division: mitosis, which produces identical daughter cells for growth and repair, and meiosis, which halves the chromosome number to make gametes. Understanding when chromosomes replicate, when they separate, and how many divisions occur answers most exam questions on this unit.

facts.label: Interphase
facts.value: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation) — chromosomes duplicate but do not yet appear as separate structures

facts.label: Mitosis
facts.value: One division, two identical diploid daughter cells; growth, repair, asexual reproduction

facts.label: Meiosis
facts.value: Two divisions, four haploid cells with half the chromosome number; gamete formation

blocks.text: The cell cycle is the ordered series of events from one cell division to the next. Interphase occupies most of the cycle: during G1 the cell grows, makes proteins and increases its organelles; during S phase each chromosome is replicated so that it consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere; during G2 the cell checks the replicated DNA and builds the machinery needed for division. The cell then enters the M phase — mitosis followed by cytokinesis. A cell that permanently leaves the cycle enters a resting stage called G0; neurons, for example, never divide in normal circumstances. Crucially, DNA replicates during S phase but the chromosomes do not separate until anaphase, which is why a replicated chromosome still counts as one chromosome until the chromatids part.

items.meaning: The complete sequence of events from one cell division to the next, including interphase and M phase.
G1 + S + G2: the cell grows and duplicates its DNA but does not yet divide.
Identical copies of a replicated chromosome joined at the centromere; each is counted as one chromosome until separation.
The constricted region holding sister chromatids together and attaching to spindle fibres.
A resting stage in which cells leave the division cycle without dividing.

items: Interphase is NOT a resting phase — it is metabolically the busiest part of the cycle.
Chromosomes replicate in S phase; the number of centromeres (and so chromosomes) does not double until chromatids separate.
A human cell has 46 chromosomes; after S phase it still has 46 chromosomes, but each now consists of two chromatids — 92 chromatids in total.
Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells; meiosis occurs only in reproductive organs to form gametes.
The cell cycle is regulated by checkpoints; faulty checkpoints allow uncontrolled division — cancer.

items.text: Skin cells divide continuously to replace worn surface cells — mitosis in a G1-S-G2-M loop of about a day.
items.note: Growth and repair both depend on mitosis producing genetically identical cells.

items.text: The liver can exit the cycle into G0 and re-enter it after injury.
items.note: G0 explains why some tissues regenerate while neurons essentially never do.

blocks.text: Mitosis is a single division that separates sister chromatids, producing two daughter cells genetically identical to the parent and to each other. In prophase the duplicated chromosomes condense and become visible, the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle fibres form. During metaphase the chromosomes line up on the equator, attached to spindle fibres by their centromeres. In anaphase the centromeres divide and the sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles — each chromatid now counts as an individual chromosome. Telophase reverses prophase: chromosomes decondense, nuclear envelopes reform around each group, and cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm — a cleavage furrow in animal cells, a cell plate in plant cells.

items: Prophase: chromosomes condense, spindle forms, nuclear envelope disappears.
Metaphase: chromosomes lie on the equatorial plate, one chromatid of each facing each pole.
Anaphase: centromeres split, chromatids move to opposite poles — the chromosomes double in number temporarily.
Telophase: two nuclei re-form; chromosomes unwind.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm; plant cells build a cell plate because the wall prevents furrowing.
Mitosis maintains the chromosome number: 2n -> 2n.

items.text: Root tip cells in mitosis: stained cells show all four stages, with metaphase figures having chromosomes aligned at the equator.
items.note: Onion root tip is the standard preparation because the meristem divides rapidly.

items.text: Wound healing: cells at the edge re-enter the cycle and divide by mitosis until the gap is closed.
items.note: Growth, repair and asexual reproduction all rely on identical daughter cells.

items.meaning: Division of the nucleus producing two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Structure of microtubule fibres that separates chromatids during division.
Division of the cytoplasm following nuclear division.
New cell wall formed between plant daughter cells during cytokinesis.

blocks.text: Meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number of the parent cell. It involves two successive divisions following a single replication. In meiosis I homologous chromosomes pair up, exchange segments (crossing over) and then separate, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome of each pair — this is the reduction step, 2n to n. Meiosis II resembles mitosis: sister chromatids separate, giving four haploid cells. Crossing over in prophase I shuffles genetic material, and the independent orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I produces new combinations — together these are the sources of genetic variation. Because four genetically different cells form from one parent cell, meiosis is also called reduction division followed by equational division.

items: Meiosis I separates HOMOLOGOUS CHROMOSOMES; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
Crossing over in prophase I exchanges segments between homologues, creating new allele combinations.
Four haploid cells form from one diploid parent cell; chromosome number is halved: 2n -> n.
Gametes are haploid (human: 23 chromosomes); fusion of gametes at fertilisation restores diploidy (46).
Meiosis introduces variation — essential for evolution; mitosis produces clones — essential for growth.

items.text: Human sperm: meiosis in the testes gives four haploid sperm from each spermatocyte, each with 23 chromosomes.
items.note: One oocyte gives one ovum plus polar bodies — the cytoplasm is conserved for the egg.

items.text: 2n = 4 cell through meiosis: after meiosis I two cells with n = 2; after meiosis II four cells with n = 2.
items.note: Counting chromosomes at each stage shows exactly where the reduction happens.

items.meaning: Two-stage division halving the chromosome number, producing four haploid cells.
Meiosis I, in which homologous pairs separate and 2n becomes n.
Exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I, creating variation.
Pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the same genes in the same positions.
One set of chromosomes, as in gametes; diploid (2n) is two sets.

blocks.text: The two divisions differ in purpose and in outcome. Mitosis conserves the chromosome number and produces identical cells; it underlies growth, tissue repair and asexual reproduction, so any organism that maintains its body uses it constantly. Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces genetically diverse cells; it underlies sexual reproduction. Without meiosis, chromosome number would double every generation after fertilisation. Without mitosis, an embryo could never grow into an adult. The exam favourite is a comparison table: number of divisions, products, chromosome number, and genetic variation — learn it as four paired contrasts.

items: Mitosis: 1 division, 2 identical diploid cells, no variation, for growth and repair.
Meiosis: 2 divisions, 4 different haploid cells, variation by crossing over and independent assortment, for gametes.
Chromosome number is maintained by mitosis and halved by meiosis; fertilisation doubles it back.
Only meiosis shows pairing of homologues and crossing over.
Errors in meiosis (non-disjunction) produce gametes with wrong chromosome numbers — aneuploidy.

items.text: Alternation: gametes (n) -> fertilisation -> zygote (2n) -> mitosis -> adult (2n) -> meiosis -> gametes (n).
items.note: The halving and doubling keep the species chromosome number constant across generations.

items.text: Down syndrome results from a gamete carrying an extra chromosome 21 after meiotic non-disjunction.
items.note: A concrete consequence of errors during meiosis I or II.

figures.caption: Figure: Stages of mitosis
figures.description: Four stages in order: prophase (condensed chromosomes, spindle forming), metaphase (chromosomes on the equator), anaphase (chromatids pulled apart), telophase (two nuclei forming) followed by cytokinesis.

figures.caption: Figure: Meiosis I and II
figures.description: Meiosis I: homologues pair at metaphase I and separate, halving the number. Meiosis II: chromatids separate as in mitosis, giving four haploid cells.

keyPoints: The cell cycle = interphase (G1, S, G2) + M phase (mitosis + cytokinesis).
DNA replicates in S phase; chromosomes separate only at anaphase.
Mitosis: one division, two genetically identical diploid cells — growth, repair, asexual reproduction.
Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically different haploid cells — gamete formation.
Meiosis I is the reduction division because homologous chromosomes separate.
Crossing over in prophase I and independent assortment create genetic variation.
Fertilisation restores diploidy, keeping the species chromosome number constant.
Cytokinesis is cytoplasmic division: cleavage furrow in animals, cell plate in plants.
examFocus: Sequence questions on mitosis need the four stages in order with one defining event each — condensation, alignment, separation, re-formation.
'Why is meiosis called reduction division?' expects: homologues separate, chromosome number halved from 2n to n in meiosis I.
Chromosome-count questions hinge on centromere counting: replication does not increase the chromosome number.
Comparison questions want four contrasts: divisions, products, chromosome number, variation.

vocabulary.meaning: G1, S and G2 — growth and DNA replication before division.
Identical halves of a replicated chromosome.
Exchange of segments between homologues during prophase I.
Meiosis I; halving of the chromosome number.
Division of the cytoplasm after nuclear division.

questions.prompt: DNA replication occurs during which phase of interphase?
questions.explanation: S (synthesis) phase is when each chromosome is duplicated into two joined sister chromatids; G1 is growth and G2 is final preparation.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing M phase — the chromosomes were duplicated earlier and merely become visible in prophase.

questions.prompt: During which stage of mitosis do the centromeres divide and the chromatids separate?
questions.explanation: Anaphase begins when centromeres split and spindle fibres pull the sister chromatids to opposite poles.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing metaphase, where chromosomes only align on the equator — separation has not started.

questions.prompt: Meiosis is called reduction division because:
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I, so the daughter cells have half the parent's chromosome number (2n to n).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'four cells are formed' — that is an outcome of meiosis, not the reason for the name.

questions.prompt: After the S phase of interphase, a human cell with 46 chromosomes contains:
questions.explanation: Replication doubles the chromatids but not the centromere count; a chromosome is counted by its centromere until chromatids separate.
questions.commonMistake: Counting 92 chromosomes — the number of centromeres has not changed.

questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes pair and exchange segments in prophase I, creating new allele combinations — it cannot occur in mitosis because homologues never pair there.
questions.commonMistake: Saying prophase of mitosis — pairing of homologues is unique to meiosis.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: mitosis produces ________ daughter cells with the ________ chromosome number, while meiosis produces ________ haploid cells.
questions.explanation: Mitosis is equational (2n to 2n, two cells); meiosis involves reduction then equational division, giving four n cells.
questions.commonMistake: Swapping the products of the two divisions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in plant cells cytokinesis occurs by the formation of a ________, whereas animal cells form a ________.
questions.explanation: The rigid cell wall prevents furrowing in plants, so a new wall builds outward from the centre; animal cells pinch inwards.

questions.prompt: Name the four stages of mitosis in order and state the key event of each.
questions.answer: Prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks down. Metaphase — chromosomes align on the equatorial plate attached to spindle fibres. Anaphase — centromeres divide and sister chromatids move to opposite poles. Telophase — chromosomes decondense and two nuclear envelopes re-form, followed by cytokinesis.
questions.explanation: Each stage is defined by one structural event; ordering them correctly earns the sequence marks.
questions.commonMistake: Describing chromatids separating in metaphase — alignment is metaphase, separation is anaphase.

questions.prompt: Give three ways in which meiosis I differs from mitosis.
questions.answer: (1) In meiosis I homologous chromosomes pair up and separate; in mitosis they act independently and never pair. (2) Meiosis I halves the chromosome number (2n to n); mitosis preserves it (2n to 2n). (3) Crossing over in prophase I of meiosis generates new combinations of alleles; mitosis produces genetically identical cells with no new combinations.
questions.explanation: The three contrasts — pairing, chromosome number and variation — cover the marking points typically allocated.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only the number of cells produced without explaining the chromosome behaviour.

questions.prompt: State the significance of mitosis and of meiosis in the life of an organism.
questions.answer: Mitosis is significant for growth: it increases cell number while keeping the chromosome number and genetic constitution constant, so it also effects tissue repair and replaces worn cells, and it underlies asexual reproduction. Meiosis is significant for sexual reproduction: it halves the chromosome number so that gametes carry one set, preventing the doubling of chromosomes at each generation, and by crossing over and independent assortment it produces genetically diverse gametes which are the raw material for evolution.
questions.explanation: Each division answers the 'why does the organism need it' question — continuity (mitosis) versus variation and chromosome constancy (meiosis).
questions.commonMistake: Saying meiosis 'produces variation' without linking it to sexual reproduction and evolution.

questions.prompt: A cell with 2n = 6 passes through meiosis. Describe the chromosome behaviour at meiosis I and meiosis II, and state the chromosome number in each of the four products.
questions.answer: Before meiosis, DNA replicates, so the cell has 6 chromosomes each with two chromatids. In meiosis I the three homologous pairs line up at the equator; homologues separate and move to opposite poles, so each daughter cell receives 3 chromosomes, each still consisting of two chromatids — the number is halved from 6 to 3. In meiosis II the centromeres divide and the chromatids separate, so each of the four final cells contains 3 single-chromatid chromosomes. All four products are haploid with n = 3.
questions.explanation: The reduction happens at meiosis I when homologues part; meiosis II only separates the chromatids, so no further reduction occurs.
questions.commonMistake: Halving again at meiosis II and reporting n = 1 or 1.5 — meiosis II is equational, not reductional.

questions.prompt: Why is interphase described as a 'resting phase' historically, and why is that name misleading?
questions.answer: Interphase was called a resting phase because no chromosomes were visible under the microscope, suggesting inactivity. The name is misleading: interphase is the most metabolically active part of the cell cycle — the cell grows, synthesises proteins and organelles, replicates its DNA during S phase, and expends substantial energy. Only the appearance of the nucleus, which remains intact with no visible chromosomes, is 'quiet'; at the molecular level the cell is busy preparing for division.
questions.explanation: The historical name comes from microscopic appearance, not physiology; the answer must contrast appearance with measured metabolic activity.
questions.commonMistake: Agreeing that nothing happens in interphase — DNA replication alone contradicts that.
